findings.title: Tracking tags with no consent tool in page source
findings.detail: Tracking tags were found (Google Analytics / Tag Manager, Meta Pixel, Hotjar, Klaviyo) but no consent management platform was detected in the page source. A consent tool loaded through a tag manager would not be visible to this check.

cost.label: £22,000 to £88,000, from comparable published ICO fines for a business your size (£1M–£10M)

fix.steps: Add a consent banner (a CMP such as Cookiebot, CookieYes or your platform's own) and load tracking tags only after someone accepts.

findings.title: No cookie information identified
findings.detail: No cookie policy page was found and the privacy notice does not explain cookies. Users must be given clear information about the cookies a site uses.

cost.label: £5,500 to £19,800, from comparable published ICO fines for a business your size (£1M–£10M)

fix.steps: Add a cookie policy page (or a cookies section in your privacy notice) listing each cookie, who sets it, what it is for and how long it lasts. Link it from the footer and the banner.
fix.paste:
Cookies we use
• Strictly necessary: [name], [purpose], [duration]
• Analytics (only with your consent): [name], [provider], [purpose], [duration]
• Advertising (only with your consent): [name], [provider], [purpose], [duration]
You can change your choice at any time: [Cookie settings]

findings.title: Privacy notice: required information not evidenced
findings.detail: The notice text does not appear to cover: lawful basis for each use; how long data is kept; individual rights; right to complain to the ico; who data is shared with; international transfers. This is a keyword check, so review the notice to confirm.

cost.label: £5,500 to £19,800, from comparable published ICO fines for a business your size (£1M–£10M)

fix.steps: Add the missing sections to your privacy notice.
fix.paste:
Who we are: Brightside Home [Ltd], [address], [contact email]
What we use your data for, and our lawful basis for each
Who we share it with
International transfers
How long we keep it
Your rights (access, correction, erasure, objection)
You can complain to the Information Commissioner's Office at ico.org.uk

findings.title: Pre-ticked marketing consent box
findings.detail: A checkbox that appears to relate to marketing is ticked by default. Consent needs a clear affirmative action, so a pre-ticked box does not provide valid consent.
findings.excerpt: Send me offers and news from Brightside Yes, I'd also like offers from selected partners Join © 2026 Brightside Home

cost.label: £27,500 to £110,000, from comparable published ICO fines for a business your size (£1M–£10M)

fix.steps: Untick every marketing box by default. Use a separate box for each channel (email, text) and drop any "partners" box.
fix.paste: <label><input type="checkbox" name="email_marketing"> Email me offers and news from Brightside Home. Unsubscribe any time.</label>

findings.title: Sign-up form without a privacy link
findings.detail: An email sign-up form was found but no link to the privacy notice was identified on the same page.

cost.label: £5,500 to £19,800, from comparable published ICO fines for a business your size (£1M–£10M)

fix.steps: Add a privacy link directly under the form.
fix.paste: See our privacy notice for how we use your details.

findings.title: Company registration details not identified
findings.detail: No company number or place of registration was found. Limited companies must show their registered name, number, place of registration and registered office on their website.

fix.steps: Add your registered company details to the footer of every page.
fix.paste: Brightside Home Ltd. Registered in England and Wales, company number [number]. Registered office: [address].

findings.title: No geographic address identified
findings.detail: No UK postal address was found on the pages reviewed. Online traders must give a geographic address.

fix.steps: Add a geographic postal address to the footer or contact page.

findings.title: No terms and conditions found
findings.detail: The site appears to sell to consumers, but no terms and conditions page was linked from the homepage. Consumers must be given key information before they buy, including the right to cancel, and the terms should be easy to find.

cost.label: Up to £1,000,000 for a business your size (higher of £300k or 10% of turnover, DMCCA 2024)

fix.steps: Publish terms and conditions and link them in the footer and at checkout.

findings.title: "10% off" for signing up, but the form never says it means marketing emails
findings.detail: The discount is only given in return for an email address, but the form doesn't tell people they are agreeing to receive marketing. Offering a reward for signing up is allowed, but the consent behind it has to be informed: say plainly what they will get, how often, and that they can unsubscribe.
findings.ruleRef: PECR Reg 22; UK GDPR Art 4(11) and 7

case.name: Poxell Ltd
case.summary: Poxell first came to the attention of the Commissioner in April 2022 as part of an investigation formed to assess and analyse complaint trends in relation to the energy and home improvements sector. The investigation established that between 31 March 2022 and 20 July 2022, Poxell made 2,647,805 unsolicited direct marketing calls in breach of regulations 21 and 24 of PECR.

cost.label: £27,500 to £110,000, from comparable published ICO fines for a business your size (£1M–£10M)

fix.steps: Say next to the button what people are signing up to, and that they can unsubscribe.
fix.paste: Sign up for emails about new products and offers from Brightside Home. Unsubscribe any time. See our privacy notice.

findings.title: Phone number collected, but the wording never mentions texts
findings.detail: This form asks for a mobile number, but nothing near it says you will send marketing texts. Consent for texts has to be specific: people need to know they are agreeing to SMS, not just email. This is the exact gap in the HelloFresh fine.

case.name: HelloFresh (Grocery Delivery E-Services UK Ltd)
case.summary: About 79M marketing emails and 1M texts. Consent was bundled with an age confirmation, never mentioned texts, and did not say marketing would continue for 24 months after cancellation. Some people were contacted after asking it to stop.

cost.label: £27,500 to £110,000, from comparable published ICO fines for a business your size (£1M–£10M)

fix.steps: Add wording that names texts, with a separate tick box for SMS, and say how to stop.
fix.paste: <label><input type="checkbox" name="sms_marketing"> Text me offers and news from Brightside Home. Reply STOP to opt out any time.</label>

case.summary: About 79M marketing emails and 1M texts. Consent was bundled with an age confirmation, never mentioned texts, and did not say marketing would continue for 24 months after cancellation. Some people were contacted after asking it to stop.

fix.steps: Say next to the button what people are signing up to, and that they can unsubscribe.

findings.title: Sign-up pop-up makes saying no hard
findings.detail: On this pop-up the way out reads "Unlock 15% off Unlock my discount No thanks, I prefer paying full price", which shames people for saying no; and the "No thanks, I prefer paying full price" option is 9px text, pale grey text, much harder to see than the sign-up button. Saying no to marketing should be as easy as saying yes. The CMA treats pressure like this as harmful online choice architecture, and consent given under it may not be freely given.
findings.ruleRef: DMCCA 2024 Part 4 Ch 1 (unfair practices); UK GDPR Art 7(4); CMA online choice architecture guidance
findings.excerpt: Wait! Unlock 15% off Unlock my discount No thanks, I prefer paying full price
evidence: the way out reads "Unlock 15% off Unlock my discount No thanks, I prefer paying full price", which shames people for saying no
the "No thanks, I prefer paying full price" option is 9px text, pale grey text, much harder to see than the sign-up button

cost.label: £27,500 to £110,000, from comparable published ICO fines for a business your size (£1M–£10M)

fix.steps: Add a clear close button and a neutral "No thanks" link, as easy to see as the sign-up button.

findings.title: "Reject" is hidden a layer down in the cookie banner
findings.detail: The first layer of the banner offers "Accept all" in one click, but to refuse people have to open "Manage settings" first. The ICO expects reject to be on the first layer and as easy as accept.
findings.ruleRef: PECR Reg 6; ICO guidance on cookies
findings.excerpt: We use cookies to give you the best experience and to show you relevant ads. Accept all Manage settings

cost.label: £22,000 to £88,000, from comparable published ICO fines for a business your size (£1M–£10M)

fix.steps: Move "Reject all" onto the first layer of the banner, next to "Accept all", same size and style. Keep "Manage choices" as a third option.
fix.paste:
<button class="cookie-btn" data-consent="accept">Accept all</button>
<button class="cookie-btn" data-consent="reject">Reject all</button>
<button class="cookie-link" data-consent="manage">Manage choices</button>

findings.title: Countdown timer that doesn't count down to a real deadline
findings.detail: A countdown that restarts, or carries on after its deadline, tells shoppers an offer is ending when it isn't. Falsely saying a product or price is only available for a very limited time is banned outright under the DMCCA 2024, and the CMA has taken action against Emma Sleep and Wowcher for exactly this.
evidence: The page's own script sets the deadline from the visitor's clock (for example "midnight tonight" or "now plus a few hours"), so the sale never actually ends: every visitor, every day, sees a fresh countdown.
We loaded the page twice, 2 seconds apart. Both times the timer showed 05:42:17 left, so it isn't counting down to a real deadline.

case.name: Emma Sleep
case.summary: Admitted misleading countdown timers and false "high demand" and discount claims, and gave court-enforceable undertakings to stop.

cost.label: No fine, but an upheld ruling is published under your name. Medium referral risk to Trading Standards if it continues.

fix.steps: Only show a countdown when there is a real, fixed end date, the same for every visitor. Take the offer down when it ends, and don't re-run it straight away.
fix.paste: Sale ends 23:59 on [day date month]. Offer terms

findings.title: Always-on claim in your announcement bar: best, biggest, no.1 or similar
findings.detail: "The UK's No.1 home brand" sits in the announcement bar, so every visitor sees it on this page whatever campaign is running. Under the CAP Code a "best" or "No.1" claim needs evidence that compares you with the whole market, kept up to date. Hold that evidence before the claim goes live, or soften the wording.

case.name: HGVT Ltd
case.summary: A website and pages for Heavy Goods Vehicle (HGV) training service providers made misleading claims about HGV test pass rates, the nature of a promotion and being the largest and best rated HGV training provider. The ad also falsely implied they were acting for purposes outside their business.
case.action: The ads must not appear again in the form complained of. The ASA told HGVT Ltd not to make “up to” claims unless a significant proportion of items were available at the advertised maximum discount, to ensure that seasonal offers and pass rate claims were not misleading, and that all such claims could be substantiated.

cost.label: No fine, but an upheld ruling is published under your name. Medium referral risk to Trading Standards if it continues.

fix.steps: Keep current, independent evidence that you are No.1 across the market (for example sales data), and say what it is based on. Or soften it.

findings.title: Always-on claim in your announcement bar: awards, memberships or origin
findings.detail: "Award-winning homeware" sits in the announcement bar, so every visitor sees it on this page whatever campaign is running. Under the CAP Code an award or endorsement needs to be real, current and named (who gave it, and when). Hold that evidence before the claim goes live, or soften the wording.

cost.label: No fine, but an upheld ruling is published under your name. Medium referral risk to Trading Standards if it continues.

fix.steps: Name the award, who gave it, and the year, and only while it's current.

findings.title: Always-on claim in your announcement bar: environmental claim
findings.detail: "100% eco-friendly packaging" sits in the announcement bar, so every visitor sees it on this page whatever campaign is running. Under the CAP Code an environmental claim needs evidence across the product's whole life, and absolute words like "eco-friendly" need the strongest proof. Hold that evidence before the claim goes live, or soften the wording.

case.name: Virgin Atlantic Airways Ltd t/a Virgin Atlantic
case.summary: A radio ad for Virgin Atlantic included the unqualified claim "100% sustainable aviation fuel", which gave a misleading impression of the fuel's environmental impact.

cost.label: No fine, but an upheld ruling is published under your name. Medium referral risk to Trading Standards if it continues.

fix.steps: Replace absolute green words with a specific, provable fact.

findings.title: Only 5-star reviews are shown
findings.detail: The review widget on this page is set to show only top-rated reviews (data-stars="5"). Showing only the best reviews without saying so gives a false picture of what customers think, which the DMCCA 2024 bans outright.
findings.ruleRef: DMCCA 2024 Sch 20 (fake reviews); CMA fake reviews guidance

case.name: Google
case.summary: Agreed to sanction businesses that boost star ratings with fake reviews and to warn consumers on their profiles.

cost.label: Up to £1,000,000 for a business your size (higher of £300k or 10% of turnover, DMCCA 2024)

fix.steps: Show all genuine reviews, low ratings included, in date order by default. If you filter, say so clearly next to the reviews.
fix.paste: Showing all [number] reviews from verified buyers, newest first.

findings.title: No statement on how reviews are collected and checked
findings.detail: Reviews are shown (Trustpilot), but nowhere on the site says how they are collected, whether they come from verified buyers, or whether any are filtered out. Since April 2025 businesses must take reasonable steps to keep fake and misleading reviews off their site, and the CMA expects a clear, published policy.
findings.ruleRef: DMCCA 2024 Sch 20 (fake reviews); CMA fake reviews guidance

case.name: Google
case.summary: Agreed to sanction businesses that boost star ratings with fake reviews and to warn consumers on their profiles.

cost.label: Up to £1,000,000 for a business your size (higher of £300k or 10% of turnover, DMCCA 2024)

fix.steps: Publish a short review policy and link it next to your reviews.
fix.paste: About our reviews: we invite every customer to review after delivery and publish all genuine reviews, good and bad. We never pay for reviews or remove them for being negative. We check reviews for fakes using [method] and remove any that don't meet our policy.

findings.title: Influencer or affiliate page with no "Ad" label
findings.detail: This page has influencer-style wording ("Hi lovelies") and a personal discount code ("Use code SOPHIE15") and affiliate tracking links, but no "Ad", "Paid partnership" or affiliate label. Paid-for content must be obviously identifiable as advertising before people start reading. The brand is responsible alongside the influencer.
findings.excerpt: Hi lovelies! These are the pieces I can't stop styling. Honestly the best lamp I've ever owned. Rattan table…
evidence: a personal discount code ("Use code SOPHIE15")

case.name: Harnbury Holdings Ltd (San Carlo)
case.summary: An influencer post paid for with free food and drink was not labelled as an ad.

cost.label: No fine, but an upheld ruling is published under your name. High referral risk to Trading Standards if it continues.

fix.steps: Put "Ad" or "Paid partnership with Brightside Home" at the very top of the page, before any content. Add "affiliate link" next to any paid links.
fix.paste: Ad · Paid partnership with Brightside Home
